items.title: Player interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2012
items.q: She and Hank Leo are good friends too, and I was talking to her one day and I was telling her, “oh Hank’s coming down.”

ctx.x: The one time my wife and I went was actually shortly before Katrina. And we had that experience of walking, it was somewhere near Bourbon Street, but we could hear this music, and we followed the sound, and on the street corner were these kids playing. And I remember they were doing “Stand by Me,” but they had the — and it was so great. And I don’t know if I was naïve in feeling I’m witnessing something that’s been going on for many, many years, and isn’t it great that it’s still happening. I mean is that a naïve —

No. I think. No, not at all. And I think that that’s again, like — how do I want to describe it — New Orleans, it’s like you see all these progressive things going on maybe, in the city, and then, I mean I think about this from time to time, but then like I’ll go to gigs, week after week after week, and I’m playing songs, obviously we are reinterpreting them over and over and over again, but playing songs from the 1920’s and the 1930’s, the same songs over and over again. So what I mean by that is that the…

you know, you can’t rush good food. You know what I mean? That’s just like the way people are. So yeah, so people just do things the way their mom did them, their grandmothers did them, their grandmother’s grandmother did them. You know. But that’s part of what makes it great too. And so, but then you have people who think that’s like the craziest thing, to keep doing things the same way you would for a hundred years. People are like why would you do that? But then I guess it goes to what your value systems are.
